bib.title: ARPO:End-to-End Policy Optimization for GUI Agents with Experience Replay

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "ARPO: End-to-End Policy Optimization for GUI Agents with Experience Replay", Fanbin Lu, Zhisheng Zhong, Shu Liu, Chi-Wing Fu, Jiaya Jia. arXiv:2505.16282v1 [cs.CV], 22 May 2025. Preprint, "Under review".

COVERAGE: All 11 pages were read, 36,706 chars in total. I read the main text fully, including the experiments, ablations, Table 1 and the conclusion. I skimmed the reference list. The paper has no appendices. The figure panels (Figs. 3–7) are charts. Only their text captions and the prose describing them were extracted, so bar and curve values not stated in the prose are not captured.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- claim: ARPO is GRPO plus a per-task replay buffer of successful trajectories. When every rollout in a group fails, one failed rollout is swapped for a stored success. This keeps reward variance non-zero and avoids vanishing advantages.
  number: none (mechanism)
  setup: Binary trajectory reward on OSWorld. The buffer has a fixed size and evicts the oldest entries. The group size is 8 rollouts per task.
  quote: "if an entire GRPO training group consists of only failed trajectories (i.e., all with zero reward), we randomly replace one of them with a previously stored successful trajectory from the buffer for the corresponding task."
  where: p.6, Sec. 3.5

- claim: ARPO on UI-Tars-1.5 reaches 29.9% on OSWorld and 23.8% on the stricter OSWorld Hard. GRPO alone reaches 26.0% and 20.9%.
  number: 29.9% / 23.8% (base 23.5% / 18.2%); GRPO 26.0% / 20.9%
  setup: 7B UI-Tars-1.5. Max 15 steps per trajectory. OSWorld has 369 tasks. Training used a 128-task subset of OSWorld. Eval temperature 0.6. Single run, no seeds or error bars reported.
  quote: "UI-Tars-7B-1.5 + ARPO 29.9% (+6.4%) 23.8% (+5.6%)" and "UI-Tars-7B-1.5 + GPRO 26.0% (+2.5%) 20.9% (+2.7%)"
  where: p.7, Table 1

- claim: ARPO also helps an older base model, UI-Tars-7B-DPO. GRPO alone gives a smaller gain.
  number: 15.6% to 20.4% (GRPO 18.3%); OSWorld Hard 11.3% to 18.0%
  setup: Same protocol as above.
  quote: "UI-Tars-7B-DPO improves from15.6% to 20.4% with ARPO."
  where: p.6, Sec. 4.2; p.7, Table 1

- claim: The replay buffer raises the final training reward and the in-domain success rate over plain GRPO.
  number: training reward 0.75 vs 0.65; in-domain success 68.8% to 81.25%
  setup: Same 128-task set. The in-domain split is 32 training tasks. The advantage appears from about step 30. A 12.5-point gain on 32 tasks is 4 tasks.
  quote: "By the end of training, the model with replay achieves a higher average trajectory reward (0.75 vs. 0.65)" and "the in-domain task success rate climbs from 68.8% with GRPO to 81.25% with ARPO, a 12.5% absolute improvement."
  where: p.7, Sec. 4.3

- claim: RL gains are mostly in-domain. Out-of-domain, GRPO slightly regresses and ARPO only roughly matches the base.
  number: in-domain base 43.8%, GRPO 68.8%, ARPO 81.25%; OOD base 55.2%, GRPO 52.08%, ARPO 56.3%
  setup: 32 tasks used for RL and "the remaining 96 as OOD tasks". The OOD tasks come from the same OSWorld set the 128 were selected from. They are not a separate benchmark.
  quote: "UI-Tars-1.5 achieves 55.2%, while GRPO slightly underperforms at 52.08%. ARPO, however, recovers generalization capability, scoring 56.3%, slightly above the base model"
  where: p.7, Sec. 4.4
  note: The intro says "hardly benefits out-of-domain agentic tasks", while the contributions say "moderate generalization improvements". The paper is inconsistent on this.

- claim: Filtering to tasks the baseline can sometimes solve raises reward, speeds convergence and increases within-group reward variance.
  number: 128 tasks kept, from filtering with 16 rollouts per task
  setup: UI-Tars-1.5 baseline. A task is kept if at least 1 of 16 rollouts succeeds. The ablation compares GRPO on the subset against GRPO on the full set (Fig. 5). Only curves are reported, with no numbers in the prose.
  quote: "A task is retained in the GRPO training set if the agent completes it successfully in at least one of these attempts. This method yields a curated set of 128 tasks"
  where: p.5, Sec. 3.4; p.8, Sec. 4.5

- claim: On-policy GRPO and ARPO beat offline preference and SFT-style methods trained on the same tasks and rollouts.
  number: ARPO 27.3%, GRPO 26.0%, KTO 24.6%, DPO 22.4%, reject sampling 21.8%
  setup: Same task set and equal rollout count. Reject sampling means SFT on positives only. DPO uses one random positive and one random negative per task. KTO labels come from thresholding the reward at 0.5. Note that ARPO is 27.3% here but 29.9% in Table 1. The paper does not explain the gap.
  quote: "ARPO achieves the highest score (27.3%), followed by GRPO (26.0%), both outperforming preference-based methods by a significant margin. Among the baselines, KTO performs best (24.6%), while DPO and Reject Sampling lag behind at 22.4% and 21.8%, respectively."
  where: p.8, Sec. 4.6

- claim: Parallelising rollouts across environments cuts epoch time sharply, because per-step latency from the OS overlaps across environments and vLLM batches the inference.
  number: per-batch rollout time 3 min (8 envs) to 19 min (256 envs); epoch time from over 6 h to about 1.2 h
  setup: Real OSWorld virtual machines with a vLLM inference server.
  quote: "the total time per epoch drops sharply from over 6 hours to just around 1.2 hours."
  where: p.8, Sec. 4.7

- claim: The training recipe uses full-trajectory multimodal context, no KL term and asymmetric clipping.
  number: up to 15 images, 64K context, 1080P screenshots; 256 parallel envs; 8 rollouts per task; 15 epochs; lr 1e-6; eps_low 0.2 and eps_high 0.3; temperature 1.0 in training
  setup: 7B UI-Tars-1.5 (Qwen2.5-VL architecture), VERL framework. The reward is binary task success (+1 or 0) plus a -1 penalty for an unparsable action.
  quote: "Our design results in a VLM model with at most 15 images input and 64K model context length" and "We remove the KL divergence loss to remove the need for the reference model."
  where: p.3, Sec. 3.2; p.6, Sec. 4.1

- claim: The authors argue the standard OSWorld evaluation can be gamed. Replacing the last action with FAIL once the step limit is reached gives credit on the benchmark's infeasible tasks. They add a stricter "OSWorld Hard" with no such replacement.
  number: none
  quote: "it will hack the rewards of the real impossible tasks defined in the benchmark."
  where: p.7, Sec. 4.1

- claim: Qualitative self-correction. The trained agent notices a wrong click (superscript instead of subscript) and undoes it with Ctrl+Z. On that one task, success went from 25% to 62.5%.
  number: 25% to 62.5% (one task)
  quote: "Notably, the success rate for the specific before and after ARPO are 25% vs. 62.5%."
  where: p.9, Sec. 4.8, Fig. 8
  note: This is one anecdotal task.

LIMITS
- The paper concedes that "strong generalization still depends on broader task diversity, carefully designed reward signals, and larger-scale training compute."
- Future work they list: more tasks, longer context for trial-and-error, and learned reward models to replace hand-crafted rule rewards.
- The training set is tiny (128 tasks) and drawn from the evaluation benchmark itself (OSWorld). The "OOD" tasks are held-out OSWorld tasks, and the task filter used the baseline model on OSWorld. Training and evaluation are therefore not cleanly separated.
- The reported results appear to come from a single run, with no variance or seeds.
- Only one model size (7B) was tested.
- Table 1 and Fig. 6 give different ARPO numbers (29.9% vs 27.3%).
- The 12.5-point in-domain gain is measured over 32 tasks.
- The abstract claims "competitive results", and the intro says "highest success rates". Table 1 does not include larger proprietary agents. The table has a "GPT-4o" column header, which the extraction renders ambiguously.
- Preprint under review. The replay buffer needs at least one earlier success on a task, so it cannot help on tasks never solved.
- Date: this is a May 2025 result. Later GUI-agent RL work may have superseded the numbers.

BUILDS ON
- GRPO (Shao et al. 2024, DeepSeekMath, ref [19]) and DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al. 2025).
- PPO (Schulman et al. 2017).
- DAPO (Yu et al. 2025, ref [28]): dynamic sampling and the clip-higher setting (eps_low 0.2, eps_high 0.3).
- UI-Tars (Qin et al. 2025, ref [16]): base model and action space.
- Qwen2.5-VL (Bai et al. 2025).
- VERL (ref [20]) as the training framework and vLLM (Kwon et al. 2023) for inference.
- OSWorld (Xie et al. 2024, ref [25]) as the environment and benchmark.
- Related RL-for-agents work cited: ToolRL (ref [15]), RAGEN (ref [21]), Sweet-RL (ref [29]), GUI-R1 (ref [24]).
- Baselines: DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023, ref [17]) and KTO (Ethayarajh et al. 2024, ref [3]).
- SFT-based GUI agents contrasted: SeeClick, Aguvis, OS-Atlas, Aria-UI.

CODE: None. The paper has no code or pseudocode. It points to https://github.com/dvlab-research/ARPO.git. The only formula is the GRPO objective with advantage Â = (r_i − μ)/σ (p.3). The extraction garbles it.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p.1): agent diagram, task completion rate and training reward. It is a quick overview.
- Fig. 2 (p.4): the RL procedure. If all n rollout rewards are zero, a positive trajectory τ+ is fetched from the replay buffer. This is the clearest picture of the mechanism.
- Fig. 3 (p.7): replay-buffer ablation, reward curves. The advantage appears from about step 30.
- Fig. 4 (p.7): in-domain vs OOD, GRPO vs ARPO.
- Fig. 5 (p.8): training reward and in-group reward variance, selected subset vs full set.
- Fig. 6 (p.9): comparison with offline methods.
- Fig. 7 (p.9): rollout efficiency.
- Fig. 8 (p.9): a trajectory with self-correction.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions were found in the PDF. The Fig. 2 text and the GRPO equation extracted garbled. Fig. 3–7 values exist only in the prose I could read. The remaining references were skimmed, not checked. The target note's frontmatter source list does not yet include arXiv:2505.16282, so this would be a new citation. I read only the first 3,000 characters of the note and did not check the rest of it for existing coverage.
